summary:
MISSION X – Interactive Space Mission Design Game

MISSION X is an educational, interactive space mission design game inspired by NASA's space exploration missions. It allows users to experience the process of planning a space mission by choosing destinations such as Earth, the Moon, and Mars. Players can design spacecraft, select scientific instruments, choose orbits and launch vehicles, and manage important resources such as mass, power, budget, and communication.

The project addresses the space mission design challenge by transforming complex mission-planning concepts into an engaging and accessible simulation. Players receive mission performance scores, engineering feedback, and a final mission report based on their design decisions.

MISSION X is important because it helps students understand the challenges of real-world space exploration, develop problem-solving and critical-thinking skills, and explore basic aerospace engineering concepts through interactive learning.
details: MISSION X is an interactive educational game that introduces users to the basic concepts of space mission planning. Users can choose a destination such as Earth, the Moon, or Mars and customise a spacecraft by selecting components and scientific instruments. They can also choose an orbit and launch vehicle. The game calculates spacecraft mass, power requirements, estimated budget, and science data capacity based on the selected equipment. It then runs a simplified mission simulation and provides a performance score, engineering feedback, and a mission report. The main benefit is that students can explore engineering trade-offs in an engaging, beginner-friendly way. For example, adding instruments can improve scientific data collection but also increases mass, power demand, and cost. The prototype was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with AI assistance. Its creative approach is to turn space mission planning into an interactive learning experience. The current calculations use simplified educational values and are not intended to represent real spacecraft specifications or flight predictions.
